questions.prompt: Three processes arrive at time zero with CPU bursts of 16, 20 and 10 milliseconds. Using non-preemptive shortest job first, what is the average waiting time in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: SJF runs them shortest-first: 10, then 16, then 20. Waiting times are 0, 10 and 26, summing to 36, so the average is 36/3 = 12 ms.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following scheduling algorithms can cause a long-running process to starve indefinitely?

options.text: Multilevel queue with round robin at every level

questions.explanation: SRTF always favours the shortest remaining burst, so a steady stream of short jobs can postpone a long job forever. FCFS and round robin both guarantee eventual service.

questions.prompt: In round robin scheduling, what happens as the time quantum grows much larger than the longest CPU burst?

options.text: It degenerates to Shortest Job First
It degenerates to First Come First Served

questions.explanation: If no process is ever preempted, each simply runs to completion in arrival order — exactly FCFS. A very small quantum has the opposite problem: context switch overhead dominates.

questions.prompt: Which technique is used to overcome the priority inversion problem?

options.text: Preemption of the higher priority task

questions.explanation: The low-priority task holding the lock temporarily inherits the priority of the highest-priority task waiting on it, so it cannot be preempted by unrelated medium-priority work. Aging solves starvation, which is a different problem.

questions.prompt: The convoy effect, where many short processes queue behind one long process, is characteristic of which scheduling policy?
questions.explanation: FCFS is non-preemptive and order-blind, so one CPU-bound job at the head of the queue holds up everything behind it, hurting both average waiting time and device utilisation.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithm requires a time quantum to be defined?
questions.explanation: Round robin is defined by its quantum: each process runs for at most that long before being moved to the back of the ready queue. The others are driven by burst length, arrival order or priority.

questions.prompt: A scheduler assigns priority proportional to a process's waiting time, re-evaluating periodically. All processes arrive at time zero and perform no I/O. This policy behaves like:
questions.explanation: The longest-waiting process always has the highest priority, so the CPU rotates among all of them in turn — which is round robin with the re-evaluation interval acting as the quantum.

questions.prompt: Two processes each alternate a 10 ms CPU burst with a 90 ms I/O burst, and their I/O can proceed in parallel. Which scheduling strategy gives the LOWEST CPU utilisation over a long period?

options.text: Round Robin with a 5 ms quantum

questions.explanation: A 5 ms quantum splits every 10 ms burst in two, doubling the number of context switches without improving overlap. Since both processes spend most of their time on I/O anyway, the extra switching is pure loss.

questions.prompt: For a fixed set of processes all arriving at the same time, which claim about turnaround time is correct?

options.text: Round robin minimises average turnaround time
Shortest Job First minimises average turnaround time
All non-preemptive policies give the same average turnaround time

questions.explanation: With identical arrival times, running the shortest job first is provably optimal for average waiting time, and hence for average turnaround time, since turnaround equals waiting plus a fixed burst.

questions.prompt: Given n processes to be scheduled on one processor, how many distinct non-preemptive schedules are possible?
questions.explanation: A non-preemptive schedule is just an ordering of the n processes, and there are n! orderings. This is why optimal scheduling by exhaustive search is impractical.
